title: Iterator: Safe In-Flight Modification & Traversal
summary: The Iterator interface methods (hasNext, next, remove). Why calling list.remove() in a loop throws an exception, and how iterator.remove() solves it.
prerequisites: The Iterable Interface & The Enhanced for-each Loop
learningObjectives: Master the core methods of java.util.Iterator<E>: hasNext(), next(), and remove()
Diagnose why calling collection.remove() inside a loop throws ConcurrentModificationException
Apply iterator.remove() to modify collections safely during traversal without exceptions
Understand the state prerequisite for iterator.remove() to prevent IllegalStateException
Leverage the modern Java 8+ collection.removeIf(Predicate) method
expectedOutcomes: Ability to explain the mechanics of safe in-flight collection mutation in placement interviews
Zero ConcurrentModificationException crashes in production batch processing pipelines

activities.title: Practical Context: Quality Control Inspector on Conveyor Line

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Quality Control Inspector on Conveyor Line
analogy.story:
Imagine an industrial conveyor belt moving manufactured components past a quality assurance inspector. The inspector picks up a component (`next()`), measures its dimensions, and if it fails specifications, pulls it off the line using their own inspection tongs (`iterator.remove()`). Because the inspector handled the removal themselves, their internal tally and sensor stay synchronized with the belt.

Now imagine a rogue floor manager suddenly runs up from behind, snatches a component off the belt by hand without telling the inspector (`collection.remove()`), causing the belt to jolt forward. The inspector reaches down expecting component #4, grabs empty air or component #5, and immediately sounds the emergency klaxon (`ConcurrentModificationException`).
analogy.keyTakeaway: Mutations during iteration must be performed through the Iterator itself so its internal tracking state remains synchronized with the collection.

activities.title: In-Flight Mutation: The remove() Contract & CME Prevention

keyTakeaways: Calling collection.remove() inside any loop triggers ConcurrentModificationException
iterator.remove() removes the last element returned by next() and updates internal bookkeeping
iterator.remove() can only be called ONCE per call to next(); consecutive calls throw IllegalStateException
Collection.removeIf(Predicate) is the modern, idiomatic Java 8+ replacement for iterator removal loops

activities.title: Purging Expired Sessions from Active Pool
activities.description: Trace an authentication session manager evicting expired login tokens using Iterator.

steps.description: Obtain an explicit Iterator<Session> reference. This gives us direct access to it.remove().
Call it.next() to advance cursor and retrieve current Session. If expired, invoke it.remove().
Bob (500) and Charlie (800) are removed cleanly without index shifts breaking traversal.

questions.question: What happens if you invoke 'it.remove()' immediately after creating an iterator, before calling 'it.next()'?
options: It removes the first element at index 0
questions.explanation: According to the Iterator contract, remove() can only be called once per call to next(). If next() has not yet been called, or if remove() was already called after the last next(), it throws IllegalStateException.

questions.question: What exception is thrown when 'list.remove(0)' is called directly inside an enhanced for-each loop over 'list'?
questions.explanation: Calling collection mutation methods directly during iteration alters modCount. When the underlying loop iterator detects the discrepancy on the next iteration, it immediately throws ConcurrentModificationException.

activities.title: Senior Engineer Interview: Why Does CME Occur in Single-Threaded Code?

qaList.question: The name 'ConcurrentModificationException' implies multithreading. Why does Java throw this exception in single-threaded code, and what architectural purpose does it serve?
qaList.answer:
Despite its name, ConcurrentModificationException has nothing to do with threads: it detects CONCURRENT MODIFICATION of a collection's structure relative to an active iterator cursor.

In single-threaded code, if you call 'list.remove(i)' during a loop, elements shift down by one index. The iterator, unaware of the shift, would skip the very next element or encounter an invalid index, leading to non-deterministic data corruption. To prevent silent data bugs, Java collections use a 'fail-fast' invariant: every modification increments an internal 'modCount'. If the iterator's 'expectedModCount' differs from 'modCount', it fails fast immediately by throwing CME. 'iterator.remove()' avoids this because it updates both 'modCount' and 'expectedModCount' atomically in tandem.

activities.title: Self-Evaluation Checklist
checklist: I understand why collection.remove() triggers CME in loops while iterator.remove() does not
I know why iterator.remove() throws IllegalStateException if called without a preceding next()
I can replace verbose iterator removal loops with modern Java 8+ collection.removeIf()
I understand the fail-fast philosophy of the modCount mechanism
